clue.text: Beds

parts.note: the single word asks for a grand kind of bed, the enumeration (4-7) pointing to the old canopied sort held up at each corner

explanation.surface: A one-word clue that could be about anything from flowerbeds to riverbeds.
explanation.walkthrough: The (4-7) count does all the work: a hyphenated eleven-letter bed with a pillar at every corner.
explanation.definitionFit: Each of these is a large bed with an upright pillar at every corner, often carrying a canopy, so it is one kind of bed.

clue.text: Party leader who raises new appeal

indicators.note: in a down clue raising something lifts it upwards, so the letters of the pieces are read from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written
O is an appealing cry, as in 'O, help me!'

explanation.surface: A political leader who drums up support with a fresh appeal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raises' turns NEW plus O (the exclamation of appeal) upside down in this down entry. David Owen led the SDP (Social Democratic Party) in 1980s Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: David Owen was a British politician who led the Social Democratic Party, so he was a party leader.

clue.text: Withdraw pamphlet after second note

indicators.note: one piece placed after another tells the solver the pamphlet comes second in the build

parts.note: re is the second note of the sol-fa scale do, re, mi
a tract is a short pamphlet, often religious or political

explanation.surface: An instruction to recall a leaflet after a follow-up memo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'note' looks like a written memo, but it is a musical note: RE, second in do-re-mi.
explanation.definitionFit: To retract a statement is to take it back, so it means to withdraw.

clue.text: Possesses nothing but three quarters of the earth

parts.note: O, the round figure zero, stands for nothing
the four quarters of the earth are the compass points N, E, S and W; three of them here are W, N and S

explanation.surface: Someone who has nothing except most of the planet.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'quarters of the earth' are the four compass points; three of them, W, N and S, follow O.
explanation.definitionFit: If someone owns a thing they have it as their property, which is what possessing means.

clue.text: They may be given to those who either book or get booked

definitions.text: They may be given to those who either book or get booked

parts.words: They may be given to those who either book or get booked
parts.note: travellers who book a seat are handed one sort of slip, and drivers booked by a traffic warden get another sort

explanation.surface: A riddle about what is handed to people who make bookings or are booked.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses of 'book' work: reserving a place earns a travel or theatre pass, while being booked by a warden earns a parking fine.
explanation.definitionFit: Passes for travel or entry and penalty notices for motoring offences share one name, and both are handed out to people in these situations.

clue.text: Rising star fails to live up to promise

definitions.text: fails to live up to promise

indicators.note: in a down clue something rising goes upwards, so the word is read from the bottom up

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A rising star who never fulfils early promise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rising star' reads as a promising newcomer, but 'Rising' turns STAR upwards in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To rat on a deal is to go back on an undertaking, betraying what was promised.

clue.text: Liar with novel ideas

parts.note: a fibber is one sense, and a person who dreams up plots for novels is the other, both under one name

explanation.surface: A dishonest person who comes up with fresh notions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' reads as 'new', but it points to fiction: someone who invents tales, whether a fibber or a writer.
explanation.definitionFit: A teller of tales can be a novelist spinning fiction or, informally, a child's word for someone who tells fibs.

clue.text: Resolution put forward on a metropolitan visit

parts.note: pert and forward both describe someone cheeky or bold
someone visiting a metropolis is in a city

explanation.surface: A motion tabled during a trip to the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resolution' looks like a formal motion, but it means determination; 'put' simply joins the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Pertinacity is stubborn persistence, the quality of holding firmly to a purpose, which is resolution.

clue.text: Give a Royal Marines' guard order to salute

parts.note: to present a thing is to give it
RM is the abbreviation for Royal Marines, and the possessive adds S

explanation.surface: Handing a Royal Marines guard its command to salute.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive on 'Marines'' gives the S, so RM plus S follows A.
explanation.definitionFit: This drill command makes a guard hold rifles upright in front of the body as a salute.

clue.text: Minister of Defence's on Sunday with boys not likely to be well off

definitions.text: boys not likely to be well off

parts.note: George Younger was the UK Secretary of State for Defence in the late 1980s; the possessive adds S
taken as written

explanation.surface: A defence minister spending Sunday with his lads, who are not rich.
explanation.walkthrough: George Younger was Britain's Defence Secretary 1986-89. Under primogeniture the eldest son inherits the estate, so the others are seldom wealthy.
explanation.definitionFit: Under the old rule that the eldest inherits, sons born later got little, so such boys were rarely wealthy.

clue.text: Vast assembly for combined Catholic and Dissenter services

parts.note: Mass is the central Catholic service
a meeting is a service of nonconformist worship, as in a Quaker meeting

explanation.surface: A huge gathering for a joint Catholic and Protestant act of worship.
explanation.walkthrough: Dissenters are English Protestants outside the Church of England, whose worship is called a meeting, as in a Quaker meeting house.
explanation.definitionFit: A large public rally of people is a big gathering, which is a vast assembly.

clue.text: Mere navy attached to army

indicators.note: one force fixed onto the end of another shows the navy follows the army in the build

parts.note: TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve
RN is the Royal Navy

explanation.surface: Merely the navy hitched to the army.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mere' looks like 'only', but it is the noun for a lake, common in the English Lake District.
explanation.definitionFit: A tarn is a small mountain lake, and a mere is another word for a lake or pond.

clue.text: Splash in so dash out

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the words so dash, which run on to give the answer

explanation.surface: A fragment of instruction to throw a splash in and then rush off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points inside 'so dash', which holds the answer; 'out' says the last two letters are left outside.
explanation.definitionFit: A splash of soda water is what is added to whisky, so the drink and the splash share a name.

clue.text: Sceptre should be treated with it

definitions.text: Sceptre should be treated with it

indicators.note: treated here means processed or worked on, so the letters of the word are reworked into a new order

explanation.surface: A royal sceptre deserves to be handled with due deference.
explanation.walkthrough: 'treated' reads as 'handled', but it rearranges the letters of SCEPTRE; the whole clue then says how such an object deserves handling.
explanation.definitionFit: A symbol of royal power ought to be handled with deference, which is the answer.

clue.text: Cash drawers still head down

indicators.note: the head letter is moved down to the bottom of this down entry

explanation.surface: Money drawers that are motionless, head lowered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head down' moves the first letter S of STILL to the end. 'drawers' looks like chests, but means drawers for money.
explanation.definitionFit: Shop tills are the drawers that hold the takings, so they are cash drawers.

clue.text: Good people phone in for lines

indicators.note: one piece placed in another means the call goes inside the saints

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for saint, and STS for saints, good people
to ring someone is to phone them

explanation.surface: Kind folk calling up in place of telephone lines.
explanation.walkthrough: Saints are the crossword's stock 'good people', abbreviated STS.
explanation.definitionFit: Strings and lines are both lengths of cord or twine.

clue.text: Woollen fabric from ram

definitions.meaning: a cloth, especially a worsted woollen material
to ram things into a bag is to cram or pack them in

explanation.walkthrough: 'ram' reads as a male sheep, a natural source of wool, but it is the verb meaning cram.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names an old woollen cloth, and as a verb it means to pack something in tightly.

clue.text: Why lists were organised

parts.note: lists were the fenced grounds for medieval jousting, set up so knights could charge at each other

explanation.surface: Asking why people draw up lists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lists' looks like written lists, but it is the medieval arena for jousting, laid out so knights could charge with lances.
explanation.definitionFit: Jousting matches with lances took place in the lists, so those contests were why the grounds were set up.

clue.text: Large barrel takes a large fish

parts.note: a tun is a large cask for wine or beer

explanation.surface: A big cask holding a big fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Tuna are large ocean fish of the mackerel family.

clue.text: Just a French mother

definitions.meaning: the French noun for a mother, written with a grave accent on its first E

explanation.definitionFit: The English adjective means no more than, and the French noun means mother.

clue.text: Frank? Cliff?

definitions.meaning: ... as an adjective means blunt and outspoken

explanation.surface: Two men's names in a row, Frank and Cliff.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective it means plain-spoken and hearty; as a noun it means a steep headland or bank.

clue.text: Material from brother Jack the Kentish rebel

parts.note: Jack Cade led a rebellion of Kentish men against Henry VI in 1450

explanation.surface: Fabric that came from a famous rebel's brother.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack Cade led the 1450 revolt from Kent, a county of south-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: Brocade is a rich woven fabric with a raised pattern, so it is a material.

clue.text: Defiant in disposition? Hardly!

indicators.note: disposition means arrangement, so the letters of the word are set out in a new order

explanation.surface: A doubt that someone was truly defiant in temperament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disposition' reads as temperament but means arrangement, reshuffling DEFIANT. Someone who fainted was hardly showing defiance, so the whole clue defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Collapsing in a swoon is the opposite of standing defiant, which the clue's closing 'Hardly!' points at.

clue.text: Sea Lord ordered dock workers

indicators.note: the word ordered here means rearranged, so the letters of the naval title are set out afresh

explanation.surface: A senior naval officer giving commands to dockers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ordered' reads as giving a command, but it rearranges SEA LORD.
explanation.definitionFit: Loaders are people who put cargo on board ships, which is work done by dockers.

clue.text: Loose-living lot soon over at Wimbledon

definitions.meaning: a quickly finished set in a tennis match, Wimbledon being the London tennis championship

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a glamorous hedonistic crowd, and read literally it is a tennis set finished in no time.

clue.text: Trunks and branch lines for Eastern and another famous railway?

parts.note: the LMS was the London, Midland and Scottish Railway, one of Britain's big four lines

explanation.surface: Railway trunk and branch lines named after old companies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trunks and branch lines' reads as railway jargon, but trees have trunks and branches. The LMS was a major British railway company from 1923 to 1947.
explanation.definitionFit: Trees of this kind have stout trunks and spreading boughs, which the railway terms describe.

clue.text: Cliff shows the evidence of his war service

definitions.meaning: a steep rocky cliff or outcrop

definitions.text: the evidence of his war service
definitions.meaning: a wound mark left on a veteran's body

explanation.surface: A veteran's cliff-face showing the marks of battle.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a bare rock face on a hillside and also the mark a healed wound leaves on the skin.

clue.text: In a harem Iran finds one of its most respected men

definitions.text: one of its most respected men

indicators.note: the letters lie in the two words harem Iran, running across the gap between them

explanation.surface: Inside a harem, Iran discovers one of its notables.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' points inside 'harem Iran', where the answer straddles the word break.
explanation.definitionFit: An emir is a Muslim ruler or commander, a man of high standing in the Islamic world.

clue.text: A French veto soon to be expected

parts.note: non is French for no, a refusal or veto

explanation.surface: A French refusal is bound to come before long.
explanation.definitionFit: Anon is an old word for shortly or before long, which is soon.

clue.text: Like the wing of a tailless lark

indicators.note: without a tail means the final letter of the bird is cut off

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Describing a lark's wing, with the bird missing its tail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lark' looks like part of the picture of a bird's wing, but it is fodder; 'Like the wing' is the definition, an adjective from Latin ala.
explanation.definitionFit: Alar is the adjective from the Latin for wing, so it means relating to wings.

clue.text: Plastic industry's advice sought by founders

definitions.text: Plastic industry's advice sought by founders

parts.words: Plastic industry's advice sought by founders
parts.note: read one way it is a slogan from plastics makers telling people to junk metal; read another, it is what metal-founders want to buy

explanation.surface: Advice from the plastics trade that company founders want to hear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'founders' looks like company founders, but means metal foundries, who buy junk metal to melt down; the plastics industry would urge everyone to junk their metal goods.
explanation.definitionFit: Waste iron and steel is what foundries remelt, and junking metal is what makers of plastics would advise.

clue.text: They don't want custom, yet presumably sell at give-away prices

definitions.text: They don't want custom, yet presumably sell at give-away prices

parts.words: They don't want custom, yet presumably sell at give-away prices
parts.note: custom means customs duties, which supporters of open trade oppose, while read literally they sound like traders who sell for nothing

explanation.surface: Odd shopkeepers who turn away customers yet sell things cheaply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'custom' looks like trade from customers but means customs duties; advocates of unrestricted trade oppose tariffs, and 'free' traders sound as if they give goods away.
explanation.definitionFit: Supporters of trade without tariffs oppose customs duties, and the word 'free' suggests selling for nothing.
